stories.headline: Rethinking Connectivity
stories.title: Rethinking Connectivity
stories.summary: A report published in Greater Kashmir on 13 October 2026, titled “CM Omar Pushes Mountain Development Policy for J&K”, highlighted the Chief Minister’s address at the inaugural session of the 13th Sustained Mountain Development Summit at SKUAST-Kashmir. The emphasis on road construction and avoiding being “penny-wise and pound-foolish” provides an opportunity to examine mountain connectivity from a broader perspective. The maxim “development begins with a road” recognizes the importance of connectivity in providing access to markets, employment, education, healthcare and essential services. In mountainous regions, however, road construction presents a complex challenge. Unlike the plains, mountains are fragile ecological systems where slope cutting and poorly planned infrastructure can disturb drainage, accelerate erosion, destabilize slopes and increase landslide risks. Roads can generate economic opportunities, but may also facilitate resource extraction while imposing substantial environmental, social and maintenance costs on mountain communities. Must every increase in transport demand necessarily be met by widening roads, cutting deeper into mountain slopes and introducing more motor vehicles into ecologically fragile areas? Rather than rejecting roads, we must reconsider their indiscriminate expansion and explore a diversified transport system that integrates modern infrastructure with traditional, locally adapted alternatives. The objective should be to identify the safest, most economical and environmentally appropriate means of connectivity for each location. Reviving traditional pathways Footpaths, mule tracks and historic trails have connected mountain villages with farms, forests, grazing grounds and markets for centuries. Many remain relevant, particularly for small, dispersed settlements and steep terrain. Improving these routes through proper steps, drainage, protective works and safe suspension bridges can preserve access without extending motorable roads everywhere. These pathways cannot replace all modern infrastructure but deserve recognition as valuable components of an integrated transport network. Equines: Living assets for mountain connectivity Horses, ponies, mules and other equines historically supported agriculture, trade, transport and communication. Industrialization has reduced their importance everywhere. Despite suffering from persistent neglect and a sharp decline in numbers, Jammu and Kashmir & Ladakh together still hold the second-largest equine population in India. They remain valuable in the difficult terrains supporting tourism, pilgrimage, agriculture, remote communities and the movement of essential supplies. Their contribution to national security in selected high-altitude areas also merits recognition. Unfortunately, these working animals and the families dependent on them often receive inadequate attention in development planning. Their declining numbers, utility and associated traditional knowledge should not be allowed to disappear through neglect. Equine healthcare, breeding, nutrition, veterinary services, livelihood support and humane working conditions must be strengthened. Appropriate load limits, adequate rest, access to water and veterinary care are essential. Recognizing equines in modern transport planning is not a return to the past, but the intelligent use of a locally adapted resource wherever geographical, ecological and economic conditions favour it. Porters, bridges and alternative technologies Human porters continue to serve isolated communities, trekkers, pilgrims and tourism in areas inaccessible to vehicles. Better equipment, fair remuneration, and insurance, safe working conditions and organized cooperatives could improve their livelihoods while ensuring that mountain tourism benefits local communities. Modern, structurally safe and flood-resilient suspension bridges can connect settlements across rivers and ravines without requiring lengthy access roads. Ropeways and goods-carrying cable systems may offer efficient alternatives across steep slopes, subject to feasibility, capacity, safety, environmental and maintenance assessments. Gravity-operated systems may also be considered where local conditions permit. Drones can deliver medicines and selected urgent supplies to remote locations, although payload, weather, battery and regulatory limitations remain. Reliable mobile networks and high-speed internet can further reduce unnecessary travel through telemedicine, online education, e-commerce and digital access to public services. These options are not universal substitutes for roads; their value lies in meeting specific needs through locally appropriate solutions. An integrated mountain transport strategy The way forward is neither indiscriminate road expansion nor blanket opposition to roads. It is an integrated transport network combining strategically planned roads with improved trails, animal tracks, and safe bridges, working equines, organized porter services, ropeways and appropriate digital technologies. Planning must begin with an assessment of actual passenger and freight needs, the requirements of remote communities, ecological carrying capacity and the full life-cycle costs of competing options. Planners must consider environmental impact, slope stability, drainage, disaster risks, maintenance, and local livelihoods from the outset, rather than treating them as afterthoughts once construction begins. For Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, such an approach could reconcile better connectivity with environmental protection, generate local employment, preserve traditional skills and reduce pressure to extend expensive motorable roads into every mountain settlement. Development must connect without destroying Roads remain indispensable where circumstances demand them. The real questions are where they are needed, how they should be constructed and whether alternative transport systems can meet particular needs more safely, economically and sustainably. In mountain regions, development does not necessarily begin with a road; it begins with intelligent, resilient and environmentally responsible connectivity. A poorly planned road can impose ecological damage, safety risks and recurring costs that outweigh its immediate benefits. Sustainable mountain development therefore requires us to look beyond roads and ask: What is the most appropriate way to connect people, livelihoods and essential services without compromising the ecological foundations on which mountain life depends? Mujeeb Fazili Former - Prof. & Head, Veterinary Clinical Complex, FVSc & AH, Shuhama, Former - Associate Director Research (A.S), SKUAST-Kashmir

stories.headline: India-Canada Relations: Overcoming a sharp dip
stories.title: India-Canada Relations: Overcoming a sharp dip
stories.summary: That India-Canada relations have overcome the sharp dip that occurred following former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and his administration’s allegations of Indian official agents being involved in the murder of Hardeep Singh Nijjar in June 2023 has once again been demonstrated by the visit of Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand to Delhi on October 13-15. During her visit Anand held talks with her counterpart S Jaishankar and was also received by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. A Canadian readout of Anand’s meeting with Modi stated that she “highlighted the significant progress made on the Canada-India joint roadmap and discussed ways to deepen cooperation between Canada and India in key areas of shared interest, including energy, education, culture and technology. It went on to note that the two leaders “... also welcomed the bilateral security dialogue that took place in India last week as part of ongoing security and law enforcement engagement at the National Security Advisor level”. Further that Modi and Anand “discussed the importance of concluding a comprehensive economic partnership agreement by the end of the year…”. The Ministry of External Affairs account of Anand’s meeting with Modi largely agreed with the Canadian version but was more expansive. It stated that the two leaders “discussed ongoing efforts to strengthen bilateral ties and expand cooperation in areas of mutual interest, including trade, science and technology, defence, security, energy, education, people-to-people ties and multilateral cooperation. Prime Minister emphasised the importance of sustaining the momentum in bilateral engagement and translating it into tangible outcomes, including through early conclusion of negotiations on a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA). They also exchanged views on regional and global developments of mutual interest”. It is good that the reset in the India-Canada ties is continuing to overcome the Trudeau shock. That process had begun with Carney’s coming to power. He obviously realised that his predecessor had simply got it wrong when he publicly accused India of being possibly responsible for Nijjar’s killing. This too when the Canadian authorities did not have any evidence which would stand up in a court of law. This has now been acknowledged by Canadian law enforcement agencies. A Canadian police official stated ““There’s no evidence to suggest through this organised crime investigation and the charges and the indictment laid forward that Indian officials were charged or involved”. Carney decided to undo the great harm that Trudeau had done to bilateral ties which were largely constructive despite continuing Indian irritants with Canadian positions on some matters like examination of visa applications of members of serving and former members of Indian security forces or of its intelligence services. Carney’s visit to India on February 27-March 2 conclusively conveyed that Canada had decided to put an end to the direction that Trudeau had taken on the bilateral ties. However, irritants can surface because of Canada’s lax attitude on offensive Khalistani propaganda towards India’s territorial integrity. This has rightly always been unacceptable to India. Freedom of expression is a precious right in all democratic societies but it can never be taken to the permissive levels as in Canada. For instance, it cannot be allowed to glorify the killers of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. Under Trudeau Canada did precisely that. It can only be hoped that this will not happen again. An Indian official brief on the relations between the two countries notes how Modi also showed that India was keen to turn the corner. It notes that during Carney’s visit “... the leaders agreed to adopt the principle of “Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam” or “One Earth, One Family, One Future” as the overarching guiding framework for the renewed India–Canada Strategic Partnership. They also underscored the alignment between India’s vision of Viksit Bharat and Canada’s Build Canada Strong agenda”. There can be little doubt that Carney’s initiative in undoing Trudeau’s disastrous approach towards India has also been influenced by US President Trump’s attempts to humiliate Canada. These began in his first term but have continued. He has not stopped from making the suggestion that Canada will be better off by joining the US as one of its constituent states. The Canadian political class and its people at large have naturally not taken kindly to Trump mocking them. They have decided to rally around the flag and Carney has had to go along with this display of nationalism. Besides, Canada has not been spared Trump’s weaponisation of tariffs. Carney decided to hit back. Consequently, he has decided to reduce Canada’s economic and commercial connections with the US and open up with other countries, including India on these fronts. India has responded well because it has too been at the receiving end of Trump’s tariffs warfare. Consequently, the two countries are currently engaged in working out a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement. That will be useful but the fact is that despite all its mounting economic troubles the US remains the world’s largest economy and every country has necessarily got to find a pathway of protecting its economic and commercial relationship with it despite Trump’s tantrums. Both India and Canada are being impacted as is the rest of the world by climate change which continues to be the principal challenge of our times though now humankind will also have to handle the rapid and unrestrained development of Artificial Intelligence. Their leaders understand this when they express the view that the planet is one. The problem here too is that Trump simply is not concerned with these issues.

stories.title: Supreme Court expands scrutiny of DGP appointment laws nationwide after Jharkhand questions Centre’s ‘special affection’
stories.summary: Court requests its amicus curiae, senior advocate Raju Ramachandran, to take the help of the Union Public Service Commission and scrutinise police laws and DGP appointments nationwide for breaches of the 2006 verdict

article_sentences: Jharkhand’s Hemant Soren government locked horns with the Centre in the Supreme Court on Thursday (October 8, 2026) over the appointment of Directors General of Police (DGPs), calling out the Union government’s “special affection” for the State when others like Bihar had “worse” appointment laws.
The confrontation erupted after the Union government moved the court against Jharkhand’s 2025 law governing the appointment of DGPs.

Appearing before a three-judge Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, for the Centre, sought a judicial declaration that the ‘Selection and Appointment of Director General and Inspector General of Police, Jharkhand (Head of Police), Regulation of 2025’ breached the apex court’s 2006 judgment in Prakash Singh versus Union of India.
The 2006 judgment had mandated insulation of the police force from political influence.
It laid down a transparent DGP appointment process followed by a minimum tenure of two years in office.
Only senior police officers with a residual tenure of six months before normal retirement could be considered for the top post.

To ensure timely compliance, State governments were directed to submit service credentials of eligible IPS officers to the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) at least three months before an incumbent’s retirement.
The Centre contended that the appointment of Jharkhand’s first woman DGP and incumbent Tadasha Mishra under the 2025 Regulation violated the Prakash Singh verdict.
Observing that the 2025 Regulation appeared prima facie non-compliant, the Bench observed that the flaw could imperil Ms. Mishra’s tenure.
However, the Bench granted Ms. Mishra an opportunity to state her case on November 3, the next date of hearing.
At this juncture, senior advocate Kapil Sibal, for Jharkhand, turned the tables on the Centre by asking why it had no similar complaints about other States.
He highlighted that West Bengal’s DGP was appointed by the Election Commission of India in March 2026 even though the officer was due to retire the next month.

stories.title: Supreme Court directs Udayasthamana pooja to be held as per Guruvayur temple practices
stories.summary: A Bench headed by Justice Aravind Kumar said the interim order prioritises the faith and sentiments of worshippers over management hurdles

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Thursday (October 8, 2026) passed an interim order that the Udayasthamana pooja must be held in accordance with the age-old practices of the famed Guruvayur Sri Krishna Temple in Kerala.
A Bench headed by Justice Aravind Kumar said the faith and sentiments of worshippers must be given precedence over management hurdles.

The petitioners led by P.C. Hary and members of traditional managing families, represented by senior advocate Guru Krishnakumar, had challenged decisions by the Guruvayur devaswom managing committee to alter or reschedule the Udayasthamana Pooja on Vrishchikam Ekadasi.

The management, represented by senior advocates C.A. Sundaram, V. Giri and advocate Rohini Musa, had argued that the performance of the rituals during Ekadasi was faced by logistical challenges posed by the massive influx of devotees on that particular day.
“I have myself stood for seven hours,” Justice Kumar said, indicating it was part of the devotional expression.
The court said it would list the main appeal in December for final hearing.

The petitioners had moved the apex court after the Kerala High Court had dismissed their pleas for a direction to the temple devaswom to ensure the conduct of the Udayasthamana pooja on Vrishchikam Ekadasi.
In October last year, the apex court had passed a similar order allowing the conduct of the pooja on the Ekadasi day which fell in the month of November.
Mr. Hary had argued that the pooja was a sacred and integral part of the temple’s ritualistic tradition.

“Until 2023, the Udayasthamana pooja was invariably performed on Vrishchikam Ekadasi day, and it is only during the last two years, 2024 and 2025, that the respondents have attempted to alter this well-established religious practice.
Such arbitrary decisions by the respondents strike at the very root of the traditional practices of the temple, which have been observed for several centuries.
The Udayasthamana pooja on Vrishchikam Ekadasi is not merely symbolic but a series of nearly 15-18 poojas that are conducted from sunrise to sunset,” the petitioners had submitted.

stories.headline: From colonial lines to protected zones: Why Indian citizens need permits to visit parts of India
stories.title: From colonial lines to protected zones: Why Indian citizens need permits to visit parts of India
stories.summary: While the system originally protected British commercial interests under the Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation of 1873, it has since been adapted to safeguard local indigenous cultures, demographic balance, and national security along sensitive international borders.

article_sentences: In four northeastern states, non-resident Indian citizens must obtain an Inner Line Permit prior to entry, regardless of whether they are visiting for tourism, business, or official work.
Arunachal Pradesh: Covering the northeastern tip of the country, Arunachal Pradesh mandates an ILP for all non-domiciled Indian citizens crossing its interstate borders with Assam or Nagaland.
Permits are issued online or at designated liaison offices in major cities like New Delhi, Kolkata, and Guwahati.
Nagaland: Nagaland enforces the ILP to protect indigenous tribal populations and preserve local customary laws.
Visitors entering commercial hubs like Dimapur or moving toward Kohima must carry valid permits.
The state offers streamlined online applications for short-term tourists.
Mizoram: Mizoram requires domestic visitors to secure an ILP before crossing its borders via road or arriving at Aizawl’s Lengpui Airport.
Temporary permits are generally issued for 15 days and can be extended for additional periods under local regulation.
Manipur: It became the fourth state to implement the ILP system following presidential approval.
Non-residents entering the state must carry a valid permit issued by the state government, obtainable via online portals or at designated entry checkposts.

Rather than applying across an entire state, several regions require special inner line permits, police clearances, or protected area permits specifically for high-security border sectors or indigenous tribal reserves.

stories.summary: Jammu, Oct 16: Jammu and Kashmir government on Friday ordered an in-depth inquiry into the matter of “alleged misconduct” by a senior Indian Administrative Service (IAS) officer with his junior woman JKAS officer after a political storm brewed over it, across the Union Territory. Commissioner Secretary, Housing and Urban Development Department, appointed as an Inquiry Officer has been asked to submit her report within 15 days. Prior to it, the surcharged atmosphere saw netizens and the politicians, cutting across party affiliations, in unison, seeking stringent action against the IAS officer. Initiated through digital media, the angst over the incident took over the entire political spectrum and social circles within 24 hours and the irate Jammu and Kashmir Administrative Service (JKAS) fraternity too joined the cause with the colleague, thus forcing the government into “direct action” mode. More prominently, the day-long developments over the matter also entailed suo-moto cognisance by the National Commission for Women (NCW) directing the Chief Secretary to probe into the matter after verification of purported video and take action (against IAS officer) if allegations proved and before that the Chief Minister taking up the matter in the strongest possible terms with the Chief Secretary and anticipating exemplary action. As a follow up to the developments, the General Administration Department (GAD) Commissioner Secretary M Raju, through order number 1654-JK(GAD) of 2026 dated October 16, 2026, accorded sanction to the “appointment of Mandeep Kaur, IAS (AGMUT: 2004), Commissioner Secretary to the Government, Housing and Urban Development Department as Inquiry Officer to conduct an in-depth inquiry into the matter of alleged misconduct by Kumar Rajeev Ranjan, IAS (AGMUT: 2010), Administrative Secretary, Labour & Employment Department, with Beenish Wani, JKAS, Assistant Director, Employment, Ganderbal, being reported in the print and electronic media.” “The Inquiry Officer shall submit her report within a period of 15 days from the date of issuance of this order,” M Raju ordered. JKAS officer Amit Vermani, Additional Secretary to the Government, General Administration Department, as per order, will be the Presenting Officer in the matter. WHAT LED TO POLITICAL TEMPEST ACROSS J&K The purported video, which led to outrage across political and social circles across J&K and even outside, showed a nasty brawl between the IAS officer, presently Administrative Secretary, Labour & Employment Department and woman JKAS officer, presently Assistant Director, Employment, Ganderbal, during review meeting, chaired by the former on implementation of Mission Yuva, on October 14, 2026. As per the purported footage viral on social media and the details emerging thereafter, the arguments between the duo began when the JKAS officer tried to explain the role of National Rural Livelihood Mission (NRLM) in implementing Mission Yuva. The IAS officer interrupted her, questioning her stance. He asked her to stop yet the woman officer took exception to interruption and shouting. As she insisted on explaining her stance, an irate IAS officer shouted and even used an abusive expression, which was strongly objected to by the JKAS officer. She also wrapped up at an inappropriate note as the IAS officer did not relent and turned to some other officer, asking for her suspension. JKAS officer, later, also lodged a complaint of harassment with the senior government officials against IAS officer, seeking action against him. WHO SAID WHAT? As the video of the brawl went viral, the clamour erupted demanding stringent action against the IAS officer with politicians leading the front. National Conference president Dr Farooq Abdullah, while alleging that the IAS officer’s behaviour lacked decency, sought his expulsion from J&K for “using abusive language against a woman bureaucrat.” He even asserted that had a similar incident happened during his time when the J&K was a state, he would have sent the (IAS) officer away on the plane. Disapproving the language used, Dr Farooq stated that the officer needed to be reprimanded. “Shouting “get out” is simply unbecoming of the conduct of a senior officer. His conduct has put all IAS officers in the spot. If he still remains here, consequences will be difficult for him,” former Chief Minister warned. Another former Chief Minister Mehbooba Mufti posted, “Such erratic and disdainful conduct cannot be tolerated. CM @OmarAbdullah must immediately take up the matter with the Government of India and demand strict action against the officer who is already facing allegations of issuing illegal gun licences.” Prior to her, her daughter Iltija Mufti, along with the viral video, had posted, quoting the IAS officer’s abusive remark to JKAS officer, “You are b…. s…, I can always talk to you like this’ - Rajeev Ranjan IAS officer abusing & threatening a lady KAS officer.” “How dare you use such derogatory demeaning language? Take your god complex & dirty slurs elsewhere. We won’t tolerate this in Kashmir. Since 2019 KAS & competent Kashmiri IAS officers are deliberately being elbowed out. There is a concerted effort to undermine local officers both in administration & police. Thereby making them subservient to outside officers lording over them,” Iltija wrote. “@CM_JnK @manojsinha_ Decency demands this man be suspended immediately. You are quick to fire Kashmiri employees. Hope you use the same yardstick here,” she continued. Peoples Conference supremo Sajad Lone noted that the video recording of a meeting where an IAS officer was screaming at a female KAS officer was scary. “This is much more than workplace bullying. But my compliments to the brave female KAS officer, Beenish. She stood her ground and upheld her dignity. We may pretend to be surprised but reality as it exists is that it is normal for such behaviour to be exhibited. Workplace bullying by officers exists,” Lone posted on ‘X’. Describing it as a vicious circle, he said, “IAS officers bully their junior officers; their junior officers bully their junior officers; and the viciousness carries on in its most lethal form on to the common masses. But I am really surprised that an army of male officers in the room and those who joined remotely in the video meeting did not stand up for their colleague. That is the real surprise.” “I would request stern action not only for today’s incident but an institutional mechanism to discourage and legally make it a crime to indulge in any sort of bullying or intimidation,” Lone demanded, asserting that this institutional mechanism should extend to masses. “It should be a crime to shout at, intimidate or bully common masses. I know of an officer who retired recently. And the top IAS babu ensured that his retirement pension and other post retirement benefits are put on hold, because of an utterly flimsy reason. Nobody will speak up,” Lone remarked. National Conference chief spokesperson Tanvir Sadiq echoed the Chief Minister as he posted on ‘X’, “Had J&K been a full state, Kumar Rajiv Ranjan would have been attached to the GAD pending a formal inquiry into his conduct. This is precisely why the fight for the restoration of full statehood is so important, and why those occupying influential positions continue to undermine it.” “The Hon’ble @CM_JnK @OmarAbdullah has taken serious note of the matter and written to the Chief Secretary to ensure that the JKAS officer faces no retribution,” he also shared. Sadiq asserted that “accountability must prevail, and no one should be allowed to misuse their position to intimidate or victimise others.” Jammu and Kashmir Pradesh Congress Committee (JKPCC) president Tariq Hameed Karra stated that he had written to “Hon’ble LG Shri @manojsinha_ Ji regarding the alleged use of street language and grossly unbecoming conduct by a senior IAS officer towards Ms. Beenish Wani, a JKAS officer.” “No bureaucratic rank confers the licence to humiliate a colleague, and no position of authority justifies such conduct. The civil services demand dignity, discipline and accountability, not arrogance, intimidation and a display of misplaced superiority,” Karra maintained, adding that the “officers who mistake authority for entitlement and resort to such rowdy conduct have no place in the civil services, at least not in Jammu & Kashmir.”

stories.headline: Apprehensions, and the Safeguards Within
stories.title: Apprehensions, and the Safeguards Within
stories.summary: The first part of this discussion traced how decades of bureaucratic control, overlapping permissions and administrative discretion constrained entrepreneurship in Jammu and Kashmir. The Ease of Doing Business Act, 2026, seeks to reverse that relationship, making government a facilitator of lawful enterprise rather than an obstacle to its establishment and growth. Chief Minister Omar Abdullah, defending the legislation in the Assembly, emphasised government’s responsibility to create an enabling environment for private enterprise. He identified administrative delays as a source of corruption and defended deemed approvals as a safeguard against indefinite official inaction. Yet, the legislation has raised apprehensions among the Group of Concerned Citizens (GCC), the Environment Policy Group (EPG) and some political leaders over its implications for ecology, urban planning, regulatory oversight, industrial land and local employment. Concerns voiced by distinguished former administrators and professionals certainly merit consideration. Having examined these concerns, I have ventured to consolidate them into seven broad categories; each to be assessed against the Act’s guiding principles, specific provisions and statutory safeguards. The objective is to distinguish genuine deficiencies from apprehensions arising out of incomplete interpretation or unfounded fears. First Objection The first objection concerns the supposed conflict between Ease of Doing Business and Ease of Living. GCC fears that facilitating entrepreneurs could compromise the interests of ordinary citizens. Yet Section 3(a), establishing the principle of Permission by Exception, explicitly states: “No prior permission, approval, or restriction shall be imposed except where justified by law in furtherance of a legitimate public interest.” Section 3(c) requires regulatory scrutiny to be proportionate to actual risks, while Section 3(g), under Economy, Equity and Environment, incorporates sustainable and inclusive development. Section 4 further obliges authorities to protect the interests of the general public rather than merely sectional or individual interests. Public welfare is thus embedded in the legislation’s guiding philosophy. Employment generation, economic self-reliance and opportunities for educated youth are themselves essential components of Ease of Living. The two objectives need not be portrayed as competing interests. Second Objection The second apprehension concerns deemed approvals and the three-year moratorium on inspections. Critics fear that enterprises could proceed without scrutiny and remain beyond regulatory reach. But the Act distinguishes administrative delays from statutory compliance. Sections 11 and 12 prescribe time-bound in-principle approvals while requiring applicable regular approvals within three years. Section 13(3) permits inspections during the moratorium upon serious complaints, subject to written approval and recorded reasons. Section 14 provides for revocation, corrective action, demolition of unauthorised construction and penalties for specified violations. Crucially, Section 30(5) requires mandatory environmental clearance before construction wherever applicable. Deemed approval is therefore not immunity from the law but protection against administrative silence becoming an indefinite veto over legitimate enterprise. Third Objection The third major objection relates to Section 22, which permits relaxation of Master Plan conditions. GCC and EPG fear that individual exemptions could undermine statutory planning and gradually alter the character of localities. While Section 22 permits relaxation of Master Plan conditions for establishing an enterprise, such deviation is intended to be exceptional, not routine. The power rests with the Executive Committee headed by the Chief Secretary, which can exercise it only with the approval of the Council Chairman, the Chief Minister. Even then, relaxation remains subject to the Negative List under Schedule II. Areas under Tourism Development Authorities are expressly excluded, while the prescribed procedure for conversion of notified saffron-belt land remains applicable. Section 22(4) further provides: “Where the approval under sub-section (1) has not been granted, the enterprise shall ensure that the Master Plan is strictly followed.” Thus, the Act places such deviations under high-level scrutiny rather than leaving them to routine administrative discretion. These safeguards, reinforced by the requirement to record reasons and protect public interests, provide a framework for exceptional relaxations while retaining accountability. Their effective implementation must ensure that environmental sensitivity, infrastructure capacity and planned development are not compromised. Fourth Objection The fourth set of objections concerns ecology, agricultural land, residential neighbourhoods, construction norms and public safety. Here, the Act contains some of its clearest safeguards. Section 30(4) expressly provides: “The provisions of this Act shall not affect the provisions or applicability of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986” The same subsection preserves the Water and Air Pollution Acts, the Forest (Conservation) Act, the Wildlife (Protection) Act and the Prevention of Ribbon Development Act. Section 30(5) additionally requires mandatory environmental clearance before construction. Schedule II strictly prohibits Red- and Orange-category industries in residential areas, while Green-category enterprises remain subject to pollution-control consent and applicable environmental laws. White-category activities, including traditional handicrafts, require no such consent. The Act also prohibits permanent structures in designated water-body zones and preserves restrictions in protected areas. These safeguards clearly counter fears of unrestricted industrial activity in residential neighbourhoods, permitting non-polluting enterprises while protecting public health, safety and residential tranquility. Concerns raised by Waheed-ur-Rehman Para and Mehbooba Mufti regarding building heights, flood vulnerability, agricultural land and seismic safety merit serious consideration. While Schedule III envisages relaxation of floor-area ratio, ground coverage and other building controls, their implementation may not be possible without corresponding amendments to the Unified Building Bye-Laws, 2021, currently in force and containing essential safeguards. The proposed amendments to these Bye-Laws are still under consideration, following the expiry of the period for inviting public objections. Since these have yet to be finalised, the concerns raised can still be collectively taken up with the government, provided a consensus emerges on the specific objections and necessary safeguards. Fifth Objection The fifth apprehension concerns freehold conversion and transfer of industrial plots. GCC fears that these provisions could encourage speculation rather than genuine industrial activity. Section 28(1), however, permits freehold conversion only after an industrial unit has remained operational and functional for five years, subject to conditions prescribed under the Industrial Policy. Sections 27 and 28 similarly regulate reassignment, subleasing and sale. The principal purpose of freehold conversion is to enable entrepreneurs to offer their industrial land as effective collateral security to banks, improving access to institutional finance without mortgaging residential houses or ancestral properties. Far from being a novel concession, this practice has existed in several states for years, including Delhi since 2005. The land nevertheless retains its industrial character, with its use governed by applicable industrial land-use conditions. Sixth Objection The sixth set of concerns involves educational institutions and third-party certification. Sections 19 and 20, permit relaxation of specified infrastructure requirements and shared use of playgrounds, libraries and laboratories. Such arrangements need not compromise educational quality, provided essential academic and safety standards are maintained. Similarly, Section 23 recognises professionals empanelled elsewhere, subject to notified rules. Professional certification does not extinguish applicable safety obligations; the rules can ensure verification, accountability and consequences for negligent certification. Seventh Objection The seventh objection concerns local employment and distribution of economic benefits, particularly emphasised by M. Y. Tarigami. It would be incorrect to suggest that the legislation overlooks opportunities for Jammu and Kashmir residents. Section 32 empowers the Executive Committee, with approval of the Council Chairman, to prescribe reservation of a percentage of vacancies for domicile candidates in enterprises employing more than ten persons. It also provides for penalties and specified exemptions. Although the percentage remains to be prescribed, the statutory mechanism exists and deserves effective implementation. The demand for substantial amendments must be supported by genuine deficiencies, not apprehensions already addressed by the Act. The government should welcome constructive suggestions from GCC, EPG and others while framing implementation rules, without allowing misplaced concerns to impede reform. Experience also raises a pertinent question: if decades of elaborate permissions and regulatory controls failed to prevent unplanned development and commercialisation of residential neighbourhoods, how would retaining the same system ensure better protection? What matters is transparent regulation, effective enforcement and accountability. Meanwhile, Jammu and Kashmir cannot afford further delay in creating opportunities for its educated and skilled youth. Their continuing migration in search of livelihoods is becoming a social tragedy, leaving ageing parents without their companionship and care, weakening family bonds and distancing a generation from its roots. We cannot continue educating our children merely to see their talent and enterprise enrich economies elsewhere. The industrial community seeks no exemption from environmental, safety or public-interest obligations. It seeks freedom from arbitrary discretion, overlapping permissions and needless delays, while remaining equally committed to preserving our ecology, resources and cultural inheritance. The choice before Jammu and Kashmir is not between entrepreneurship and ecology, or Ease of Doing Business and Ease of Living, but between perpetuating bureaucratic control and establishing transparent, responsible and accountable regulation. The government must now move swiftly to frame the necessary rules, enforce statutory safeguards and translate the Act’s promise into opportunities on the ground. The stakes extend far beyond economic growth. Every year, more of our educated and skilled youth leave in search of opportunities, taking their talent elsewhere while ageing parents endure the pain of separation. We cannot continue producing graduates for other economies while our own remains deprived of their potential. Let us create the conditions for this generation to innovate, invest and build dignified futures in its own homeland. The time to act is now, before the migration of talent becomes an irreversible loss of opportunity, family bonds and hope. Shakeel Qalander, prominent business leader and a civil society animator

Sections 19 and 20, permit relaxation of specified infrastructure requirements and shared use of playgrounds, libraries and laboratories.
Such arrangements need not compromise educational quality, provided essential academic and safety standards are maintained.
Similarly, Section 23 recognises professionals empanelled elsewhere, subject to notified rules.
Professional certification does not extinguish applicable safety obligations; the rules can ensure verification, accountability and consequences for negligent certification.
Seventh Objection.
The seventh objection concerns local employment and distribution of economic benefits, particularly emphasised by M. Y. Tarigami.
It would be incorrect to suggest that the legislation overlooks opportunities for Jammu and Kashmir residents.

Section 32 empowers the Executive Committee, with approval of the Council Chairman, to prescribe reservation of a percentage of vacancies for domicile candidates in enterprises employing more than ten persons.
It also provides for penalties and specified exemptions.
Although the percentage remains to be prescribed, the statutory mechanism exists and deserves effective implementation.
The demand for substantial amendments must be supported by genuine deficiencies, not apprehensions already addressed by the Act.
The government should welcome constructive suggestions from GCC, EPG and others while framing implementation rules, without allowing misplaced concerns to impede reform.

Experience also raises a pertinent question: if decades of elaborate permissions and regulatory controls failed to prevent unplanned development and commercialisation of residential neighbourhoods, how would retaining the same system ensure better protection?
What matters is transparent regulation, effective enforcement and accountability.
Meanwhile, Jammu and Kashmir cannot afford further delay in creating opportunities for its educated and skilled youth.

Their continuing migration in search of livelihoods is becoming a social tragedy, leaving ageing parents without their companionship and care, weakening family bonds and distancing a generation from its roots.
We cannot continue educating our children merely to see their talent and enterprise enrich economies elsewhere.
The industrial community seeks no exemption from environmental, safety or public-interest obligations.
It seeks freedom from arbitrary discretion, overlapping permissions and needless delays, while remaining equally committed to preserving our ecology, resources and cultural inheritance.

The choice before Jammu and Kashmir is not between entrepreneurship and ecology, or Ease of Doing Business and Ease of Living, but between perpetuating bureaucratic control and establishing transparent, responsible and accountable regulation.
The government must now move swiftly to frame the necessary rules, enforce statutory safeguards and translate the Act’s promise into opportunities on the ground.
The stakes extend far beyond economic growth.
Every year, more of our educated and skilled youth leave in search of opportunities, taking their talent elsewhere while ageing parents endure the pain of separation.
We cannot continue producing graduates for other economies while our own remains deprived of their potential.
Let us create the conditions for this generation to innovate, invest and build dignified futures in its own homeland.
The time to act is now, before the migration of talent becomes an irreversible loss of opportunity, family bonds and hope.

stories.title: Kashmir Syncretic Traditions
stories.summary: Since time immemorial, Kashmir has been the abode of many deities, Sufi saints, seers, and savants of very high spiritual splendour, intensity, and grace who enriched the culture and thought process of the people. The land has been blessed by deities Lord Shiva, Parvati, Brahma, Vishnu, Lord Ram, Sita, and Lord Krishna. Sufi saints and Rishis Lal Ded, Nund Rishi, Shah Hamdani, and Sayed Sharaf-ud-Din Rehman (Bulbul Shah) advocated the oneness of God and brotherhood through divine preachings. Kashmir has also been blessed by the Sikh Gurus, Guru Nanak Dev Ji, Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, and Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji, who also carried the same message. Buddhist monastic Guru Padmasambhav also preached in Kashmir. These noble men believed in the magnanimity of God and spread the message of universal brotherhood. Rishi Kashyap bifurcated a mountain at village Khadniyar, Baramulla, and drained Lake Sati Sar, and as a result, the Valley emerged. The Valley experiences picturesque frames in various seasons, each having its exquisite aroma. God has sanctified all the beauty of nature in the Valley, and Kashmir is indeed the Divine Land, whose beauty takes heavenly shades, from blooming spring flowers to golden autumn leaves. Kashmir, also in all its feminine beauty of crystal -clear streams and lakes, lush green valleys, and magnificent snow-capped Himalayan peaks, qualifies for the title “Paradise on Earth.” Sanskrit poet Kalidasa has written about the Valley: “The place is more beautiful than heaven and is the benefactor of Supreme bliss and happiness. It seems to me that I am taking a bath in the lake of Nectar.” Kashmir has the distinction of being home to many revered Islamic shrines, ancient Hindu temples, and historical Sikh Gurdwaras that reflect a rich example of spiritual harmony. Syncretic traditions are cultural, religious, architectural, and philosophical practices that blend different and distinct belief systems into a new, unified whole. The history of Kashmir is not adequately understood through the background of any particular religion. It is rather the history of a civilization repeatedly shaped over many centuries. The Kashmir Valley became a meeting ground of religious traditions, philosophical systems, languages, political cultures, and social practices. Brahminical traditions, Buddhism, Kashmir Shaivism, Islam, Sufism, Rishism, and later Sikh and Dogra influences did not suddenly appear one after another and disappear. They interacted with what already existed. Elements were absorbed, transformed, resisted, adapted, and sometimes rejected. Once Islam became indigenous to Kashmir, it itself underwent transformation through its encounter with the same local cultural environment. That is where Sufism and, particularly, the Rishi traditions became central. Sayed Ali Hamdani was the greatest missionary, whose personality wielded the most extraordinary influence in the spread of Islam. Sikhism did not become a demographic equivalent o f Islam or the older Hindu traditions of Kashmir, but Sikh institutions, communities, and political authority became part of Kashmir’s evolving social landscape. During the Dogra rule, the political structure changed, administrative institutions changed, and relations among religious communities acquired a new political dimension. The celestial Valley, cradled in its arms, a unique type of Hindu Mysticism and Muslim Sufism. Mysticism in Kashmir was always different; there were Hindu mystics whose principles and methods resembled or were identical to those of Muslim saints. Also, there had been Muslim Rishis who were influenced by Kashmir Shaivism and Hindu thought. Four major Sufi “Silsilas” or orders that obtained prominence between the 12th and 16th centuries were: • Qadiri Order, founded by Sheikh Abdul Qadir Gilani of Baghdad • Suharwardiya Order, founded by Shihab-al-Din Suharwardi of Persia • Shadhiliya Order, founded by Abu -al-Hasan-al-Shadhili, a Moroccan scholar • Mevlevi Order, founded by Jalal -al-Din Muhammad Rumi, resident of Wakhsh, present-day Tajikistan Another faith that evolved was Rishism. A Rishi is a sage who sees spiritual truth. Abul Fazal writes, “The most respected class of people in this country, Kashmir, is the Rishis.” Although they have not abandoned the traditional and customary form of Taqlid (following), yet they are true in their worship. Emperor Jahangir wrote, “Although they have not acquired learning and Marifa, they live a frank and unostentatious life.” The Islamic philosophy of divine unity of being (Wahdat -ul-Wujud) is not different from Hindu philosophy of non -duality (Advaita). It is not at all surprising that the Rishis constantly preached complete harmony amongst different religions and peace and understanding among their followers. If Lal Ded represents the pre-Islamic spiritual inheritance of Kashmir, Sheikh Noor-ud-Din Noorani (Nund Rishi) represents the extraordinary localisation of Islam. Linguistic syncretism connects people and ideas. Language is the core text of human life that lets us shape thoughts, build societies, and pass down knowledge across time. All faiths in Kashmir, over the entire spectrum of time, spoke the same language, “Koshur.” The Muslim and Hindu communities wore the same dress, “Pheran,” shared common surnames, had some common wedding rituals like the use of Mehendi (Henna), and referred to the bride and groom as Maharein and Mahraz. The communities together engaged in the same music and dance (Rouf, Chakri, Band Pathar). Sufi Mystical Music of Kashmir (SAMA) forms an essential part of the region’s rich mystic and classical traditions called Sufiana Kalam. The lyrics used include Hamd (Praise of God), Na’d (Cosmic sound or Divine Vibration), and mystical poetry of Kashmiri saints. The main instruments used are Santoor, Rubab, and Trumbkanari. Hindus and Muslims together participated in many religious functions. Zain -ul- Abdin participated in the festival of Vyeth Truva (ceremony marking the birth of River Jhelum). Historically, both communities carried out shrine veneration and frequented shrines of Sufi mystics and Rishis, blending Vedantic/Shaivite philosophy with Islamic Sufism. The day after the festival of Herath (Mahashivratri), Muslim neighbours traditionally visited Pandit households to offer greetings and exchange pleasantries (a custom named SALAM), symbolising communal harmony. During the Afghan rule, Jabbar Khan wanted to test the local belief that on Shivratri there is a likelihood of snowfall. He banned the celebration in the scheduled month of February and forced the community to hold it in June/July. To his shock and dismay, it snowed in the Valley on that summer day. The architectural fusion of Kashmir not only represents the adaptation of Islamic principles to local conditions but also underscores the spirit of tolerance and coexistence that has historically defined Kashmiri society. Some of the shrines, often built in a combination of Islamic and Hindu architectural styles, stand as symbols of the harmony that the Rishis sought to create in Kashmir. The wooden structure of Khanqah, adorned with intricate papier-mâché work, colourful floral motifs, and stunning wood carving, as also the magnificent Jama Masjid, are the finest examples of Syncretic Kashmiri Islamic Architecture. The indigenous secularism, traditional composite culture, and social ethos of Kashmir represented communal harmony, religious tolerance, and shared heritage among its people. Though presently people connect with the word Kashmiriyat, this word does not find mention in any important historical accounts. It was sometime in 1975, after the Kashmir Accord, that Mohd Amin (Ibn Mahjoor) had proposed that we must support a political party that is rooted in Kashmir and would retain the culture of Kashmir, and that would be Kashmiriyat. Kashmiriyat and the composite culture got threatened during the armed militancy when the exodus of Kashmiri Pandits took place on 19 January. The word Kashmiriyat has often been quoted in various debates and conferences. Kashmiris have always resisted external aggression that started with the invasion by the Mughals, but what has been more painful is that the nefarious designs during militancy were not understood. With the exodus of Kashmiri Pandits, Kashmiryat and composite culture have taken a huge hit, but all-out efforts are being taken to see to it that this cementing force is not threatened anymore. The militancy in Kashmir affected people of every faith, and tens of thousands of innocent lives were lost. More than 150 Hindu shrines across the Valley were damaged, desecrated, or left in ruins. The terrorist strikes in the Valley did not even spare holy shrines. Foreign terrorist Mast Gul and his men established a retreat near the holy Charar -e-Sharif shrine. The siege lasted for more than 60 days. The siege ended on 11 May 1995 with a fire that engulfed the shrine. 1990. To conclude, Kashmir’s Syncretic traditions were not created by a proclamation. They emerged gradually from centuries of human interaction. The Valley went through a trying time during the militancy period, and it was these traditions and values that helped Kashmir to emerge a winner, embracing people of all faiths. The manner in which people of all faiths stood by each other in total sync and harmony to fight the floods of 2014 was again a great example of Kashmiryat. Gurdwaras, Mosques, and Temples were open to people of all faiths for food and shelter. The efforts being taken for a dignified and secure return of the Kashmiri Pandits are a welcome step to revive the Syncretic Traditions of Kashmir. (The writer is a former Deputy Assistant Chief of Headquarters Integrated Staff (IT), author, and Social Activist. Feedback: sodhidalbir7777@gmail.com )
